topics.title: Social psychology and the building blocks of social behaviour

learn.hook: Why do you clap louder when the whole stadium claps? Why do you trust some news channels and not others? Social psychology studies how others shape what we think, feel and do.
points: Social psychology is the branch of psychology that investigates how the behaviour of individuals is affected by others and by the social environment — how we think, feel and act in social situations.
In the rationalised CBSE syllabus, this chapter focuses on attitudes (their nature, formation and change, and the attitude–behaviour link) and on prejudice and discrimination.
Social behaviour is shaped by social cognition — the mental processes of gathering and interpreting information about the social world — and by social influence from others.
Attitudes, beliefs and values are the building blocks of social behaviour: they shape how we judge people, events and ideas, and how we act towards them.

example.q: Riya decides to stop using plastic bags after her friends start a 'no plastic' drive. Which aspects of social behaviour are involved?
steps: She gathers and interprets information about the drive — social cognition.
Her friends' behaviour affects her — social influence.
A new attitude towards plastic is forming — a building block of social behaviour.
example.answer: Social cognition, social influence and attitude formation.

learn.reallife: When neighbours in an Indian housing society all start segregating waste, newcomers quickly do the same — social psychology in action.

topics.title: Nature of attitudes and their A-B-C components

learn.hook: 'I love cricket' (feeling), 'I think cricket builds teamwork' (thought), 'I play every evening' (action). Three sentences, one attitude.
points: An attitude is a state of the mind — a set of views or thoughts regarding a topic (the attitude object) — that has an evaluative feature (positive, negative or neutral).

The tri-component (A-B-C) model: Affective component — the emotional part (feelings). Behavioural (conative) component — the tendency to act in a certain way. Cognitive component — the thought or belief part.
Attitude objects can be people, groups, objects, ideas or issues (e.g., attitude towards online classes, towards saving water).
Attitudes are fairly stable and help guide behaviour, though they can change.

example.q: Identify the A, B and C components: 'I believe planting trees reduces pollution. I feel happy seeing green parks. I plant a sapling every monsoon.'
steps: 'I believe planting trees reduces pollution' → cognitive.
'I feel happy seeing green parks' → affective.
'I plant a sapling every monsoon' → behavioural (conative).
example.answer: Cognitive, affective and behavioural components respectively.

learn.reallife: The 'Swachh' cleanliness drives in many Indian cities try to work on all three components: information (cognitive), pride in a clean city (affective) and actual clean-ups (behavioural).

topics.title: Beliefs, values and features of attitudes

learn.hook: Rate your view on space exploration from 1 (very negative) to 5 (very positive). Your number reveals two features of your attitude: its valence and how extreme it is.
points: Beliefs are the cognitive component of attitudes and form the ground on which attitudes stand (for example, belief in democracy). Values are attitudes or beliefs that contain a 'should' or 'ought' aspect, such as moral values like honesty and hard work. Values form when a belief or attitude becomes an inseparable part of one's outlook on life, so they are hard to change.
Valence (positivity or negativity): on a 5-point scale (1 = very negative, 2 = negative, 3 = neutral, 4 = positive, 5 = very positive), a rating of 4 shows positive valence.
Extremeness: how positive or negative the attitude is. Ratings 1 and 5 are equally extreme and are more extreme than 2 and 4; a rating of 3 is the least extreme.

Simplicity or complexity (multiplexity): how many attitudes there are within a broader attitude. An attitude towards health and well-being, for example, includes many smaller attitudes (physical health, happiness, diet) — it is complex.
Centrality: the role of a particular attitude in the attitude system. A central attitude influences many other attitudes and is more resistant to change than peripheral ones.

example.q: Arjun rates his view of nuclear energy as 2, and Leena rates hers as 5 on a 1–5 scale. Compare valence and extremeness.
steps: Arjun: 2 → negative valence.
Leena: 5 → positive valence.
Extremeness: 5 is at the end of the scale; 2 is one step from neutral.
Leena's attitude is more extreme.
example.answer: Arjun's attitude is negative, Leena's is positive and more extreme.

learn.reallife: Survey agencies in India ask voters and consumers to rate views on 5-point scales — the numbers capture valence and extremeness of attitudes towards products and policies.

learn.hook: Why do you like a subject? Often it started with a teacher you liked. Attitudes are learned — and there are five main ways it happens.
points: Learning through association: a positive attitude towards one thing spreads to what it is linked with (e.g., liking a teacher leads to liking the subject she teaches).
Learning through rewards and punishment: being praised for a behaviour builds a positive attitude towards it (e.g., praised for doing yoga → positive attitude to yoga).
Learning through modelling (observation): watching others being praised or punished for holding an attitude or behaving in a certain way.

Learning through group or cultural norms: norms are unwritten rules about behaviour expected in a group or culture; over time they become part of our attitudes. Learning through exposure to information: books, the media and biographies of admired people shape attitudes.

Factors in attitude formation: family and school environment (especially in early years), reference groups (groups whose norms one accepts), personal experiences, and media-related influences (print, TV, internet — which can create both positive and negative attitudes).

example.q: Ishita sees her elder brother praised by the family for volunteering at a blood donation camp, and she develops a positive attitude towards volunteering. Which process is this?
steps: She did not volunteer herself or get rewarded directly.
She watched someone else being praised.
Learning by observing others = modelling.

learn.reallife: Biographies of people like Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam have inspired positive attitudes towards science in many Indian students — an example of learning through exposure to information.

topics.title: Attitude change: Heider's balance and Festinger's dissonance

learn.hook: You know junk food is unhealthy, yet you eat it every day. That uneasy feeling? Festinger called it cognitive dissonance — and it pushes you to change something.
points: Heider's balance concept is expressed as a P-O-X triangle: P is the person whose attitude is studied, O is another person, and X is the attitude object. Each of the three relations (P–O, P–X, O–X) can be positive or negative.

Imbalance exists when all three sides are negative, or when two sides are positive and one is negative. Balance exists when all three are positive, or when two are negative and one is positive. (Tip: multiply the signs — a positive product means balance.)
Imbalance is uncomfortable, so the attitude changes in the direction of balance.

Festinger's cognitive dissonance: the cognitive components of an attitude must be consistent (consonant). If two cognitions are dissonant (e.g., 'Junk food harms health' and 'I eat junk food daily'), one of them is changed to restore consonance (e.g., 'I'll eat junk food only once a week').
Both balance and dissonance are examples of cognitive consistency: two components or elements of an attitude must be consistent with each other.

example.q: P (Priya) likes O (Omar), Priya likes cricket (X), but Omar dislikes cricket. Is this balanced? How might it change?
steps: P–O positive (+), P–X positive (+), O–X negative (−).
Two positive and one negative → product is negative → imbalance.
To restore balance, Priya may start liking cricket less, or persuade Omar to like it, or like Omar less.
example.answer: Imbalanced; one relation must change to restore balance.

learn.reallife: Anti-smoking ads in Indian cinemas create dissonance — 'Smoking kills' versus 'I smoke' — hoping viewers will resolve it by quitting.

quiz.q: In Heider's P-O-X triangle, O stands for:
options: The person whose attitude is being studied
quiz.explain: P is the person, O is another person, X is the attitude object.
steps: P-O-X: P = the person whose attitude is studied, O = another person, X = the attitude object.
So O is another person.
Answer: Another person

quiz.q: According to Heider, imbalance exists when:
options: Two sides are negative and one is positive
Two sides of the P-O-X triangle are positive and one is negative
quiz.explain: Imbalance: all three negative, or two positive and one negative.
steps: Imbalance: all three negative, or two positive and one negative.
Product of signs: (+)(+)(−) = negative → imbalance.
Answer: Two sides of the P-O-X triangle are positive and one is negative

quiz.q: A P-O-X triangle with two negative sides and one positive side is:
quiz.explain: Two negatives and one positive give a positive product — balance.
steps: Two negative and one positive: (−)(−)(+) = positive.
Positive product → balanced.
Answer: Balanced
quiz.mistake: Thinks any negative side means imbalance.

quiz.q: A P-O-X triangle in which all three relations are negative is:
quiz.explain: All three negative is one of the two imbalanced cases.
steps: All three negative: (−)(−)(−) = negative.
So the triangle is imbalanced.
Answer: Imbalanced
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'all the same sign' always means balance.

quiz.q: Cognitive dissonance theory was proposed by:
quiz.explain: Festinger proposed cognitive dissonance.
steps: Cognitive dissonance theory was proposed by Leon Festinger.
Heider gave balance theory.
Answer: Leon Festinger

quiz.q: 'Smoking causes cancer' and 'I smoke' are two cognitions that are:
quiz.explain: They are inconsistent, creating dissonance.
steps: 'Smoking causes cancer' and 'I smoke' are inconsistent.
Inconsistent cognitions are dissonant.
Answer: Dissonant

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A person who knows smoking is harmful but smokes may reduce or quit smoking.
Reason (R): When two cognitions are dissonant, one of them tends to change to restore consonance.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; the drive to reduce dissonance explains the change in behaviour.
steps: A: a person who knows smoking harms may cut down – true.
R: dissonant cognitions push one of them to change – true.
Reducing dissonance explains the change.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link dissonance to attitude or behaviour change.

quiz.q: Case: Sana (P) admires her coach (O). The coach strongly supports early-morning training (X), but Sana dislikes it. According to balance theory, Sana is most likely to:
options: Feel perfectly comfortable with no change
Like both the coach and the training less at once
Change one relation, e.g. start liking early-morning training
quiz.explain: P–O (+), O–X (+), P–X (−) is imbalanced; changing P–X to positive restores balance.
steps: P–O (+), O–X (+), P–X (−): product negative → imbalance.
Imbalance is uncomfortable, so a relation changes.
E.g. Sana starts liking early-morning training.
Answer: Change one relation, e.g. start liking early-morning training
quiz.mistake: Fails to see the triangle is imbalanced.

teach.ask: Gappu frets: 'I love my friend, my friend loves rain, but I hate rain! Why do I feel so uneasy?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Two positives and one negative = imbalance. I might learn to like the rain — or at least the rainbows!
teach.nudge: Is a triangle with two positive sides and one negative side balanced or imbalanced?

revise.summary: Heider's balance theory uses the P-O-X triangle: imbalance (all negative, or two positive and one negative) pushes attitudes towards balance. Festinger's cognitive dissonance says inconsistent cognitions make one change. Both reflect cognitive consistency.

Cognitive dissonance and how it is reduced
remember: P: person; O: other person; X: attitude object
Positive product of signs = balance; negative = imbalance

All three negative is imbalanced

topics.title: Mohsin's two-step concept and features of the existing attitude

learn.hook: Your favourite cricketer starts eating millets and posts about it. A month later, you're trying ragi dosa. An Indian psychologist explained this in two neat steps.
points: S.M. Mohsin's two-step concept: the target is the person whose attitude is to be changed; the source is the person through whose influence the change happens.

Step 1: the target identifies with the source — the target likes and regards the source highly and puts herself or himself in the source's place. The source should also have a positive attitude towards the target.

Step 2: the source actually shows an attitude change by changing her or his own behaviour towards the attitude object. Observing this, the target imitates the source and changes her or his attitude and behaviour.

Characteristics of the existing attitude affect change: attitudes in a state of imbalance or dissonance are more open to change; extreme and central attitudes are harder to change than less extreme or peripheral ones; simple attitudes are easier to change than complex (multiplex) ones.

Direction of change: congruent change (same direction — a positive attitude becomes more positive) or incongruent change (opposite direction — a positive attitude becomes negative). An extreme attitude is especially hard to change incongruently.

example.q: Neeraj admires his elder cousin, a doctor, who has always eaten fried snacks. The cousin starts eating fruits instead and talks about it. Neeraj soon does the same. Map this to Mohsin's steps.
steps: Target: Neeraj; source: his doctor cousin.
Step 1: Neeraj identifies with and admires the cousin, who is also fond of him.
Step 2: the cousin changes his own behaviour (eating fruits); Neeraj observes and imitates.
example.answer: Step 1: identification with the source; Step 2: source shows the change, target imitates.

learn.reallife: Public health campaigns in India often feature admired sportspersons who first adopt the behaviour themselves (e.g., getting vaccinated on camera), using Mohsin's second step.

topics.title: Source, message and target factors in attitude change

learn.hook: Why do toothpaste ads show a dentist in a white coat? Who says it, what is said and who hears it all decide whether attitudes change.
points: Source characteristics: credibility (a highly credible, expert source produces more change) and attractiveness (an attractive or likeable source produces more change).

Message characteristics: the amount of information (attitudes change most when the information is just enough — neither too much nor too little); rational appeal (facts, e.g. 'saves fuel') versus emotional appeal (feelings, e.g. 'loving families choose this'); the motives the message activates (such as health, safety or status); and the mode of spreading (face-to-face messages are more effective than indirect ones like letters or pamphlets).

Target characteristics: persuasibility (people with open, flexible personalities change more easily); strong prejudices make change less likely; low self-esteem people change more easily than high self-esteem people; more intelligent people may change less easily, though sometimes they change more willingly because they base attitudes on more information and thinking.
Analysing an advertisement: identify the source (who), the appeal (rational or emotional), the motive activated, and the intended target audience.

example.q: Analyse an ad: a famous cricketer smiles and says, 'Champions start their day with this cereal — be a champion!'
steps: Source: attractive and popular, not necessarily an expert in nutrition.
Appeal: emotional — wanting to feel like a champion.
Motive activated: achievement and status.
Target: young sports fans.
example.answer: Attractive source, emotional appeal, achievement/status motive, young sports-fan audience.

learn.reallife: Government health campaigns in India pair doctors (credibility) with film stars (attractiveness) and use both facts and emotions — covering all the bases of persuasion.

learn.hook: Almost everyone says littering is bad. Yet plastic bottles still pile up on beaches. Why don't our actions always match our attitudes?
points: Attitudes predict behaviour better when: the attitude is strong and occupies a central place in the attitude system; the person is aware of her or his attitude; there is very little or no external pressure to behave in a particular way.
Also when the person's behaviour is not being watched or evaluated by others, and when the person thinks the behaviour will have a positive consequence and so intends to engage in it.

LaPiere's study (1930s): LaPiere travelled across the USA with a Chinese couple and stayed in many hotels; they were refused service only once. Later, when hotel managers were sent a questionnaire asking whether they would accept Chinese guests, most said they would not — a gap between stated attitude and actual behaviour.

Behaviour can also shape attitudes. Festinger and Carlsmith asked students to do a very boring task and then tell others it was interesting. Students paid $1 for this later rated the task as more interesting than those paid $20 — with little external justification, they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude.

example.q: Why did the $1 students, not the $20 students, change their attitude towards the boring task?
steps: Both groups said the task was interesting, which conflicted with their experience.
$20 was enough external justification: 'I said it for the money.'
$1 was not enough justification, so dissonance remained.
They reduced it by believing the task really was interesting.
example.answer: Low payment gave too little justification, so they changed their attitude to reduce dissonance.

learn.reallife: Many Indians support saving water in surveys, but behaviour improves most when households can see their own usage and there are positive consequences, like lower bills — matching the conditions for attitude–behaviour consistency.

topics.title: Prejudice, stereotypes, discrimination and their sources

learn.hook: 'People from that city are all rude.' One sentence — a stereotype, a prejudice and a possible seed of discrimination. Let's untangle them.
points: Prejudices are attitudes towards a particular group, usually negative and often based on stereotypes. A stereotype is a cluster of ideas about the characteristics of a group, assumed to be true of all its members; it is the cognitive component of prejudice and is often based on limited or incorrect information.
Discrimination is the behavioural component — negative actions towards members of a group. Prejudice can exist without discrimination, and discrimination can occur without prejudice.
Sources: learning — prejudices are learned through association, rewards and punishment, observation, group norms, family, reference groups, personal experiences and the media.

A strong social identity with an ingroup and ingroup bias can lead to negative attitudes towards outgroups. Scapegoating: a majority group blames a weaker minority outgroup for its own social, economic or political problems.

Kernel of truth: stereotypes may persist because there may be a small element of truth in them. Self-fulfilling prophecy: the target group behaves in ways that confirm the prejudice (e.g., a group labelled 'dull' loses motivation and performs poorly), keeping the prejudice alive.

example.q: Label each: (a) 'All engineers are boring' (thought), (b) feeling dislike for engineers (feeling), (c) refusing to rent a flat to engineers (action).
steps: (a) A generalised belief about a group = stereotype (cognitive).
(b) A negative feeling/attitude towards the group = prejudice.
(c) Negative action = discrimination (behavioural).

learn.reallife: The Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15) — law tackles discriminatory behaviour, while education targets prejudiced attitudes.

learn.hook: Put students from rival schools on one team for a national science fair. By the end, the 'rivals' are friends. Contact under the right conditions can melt prejudice.
points: Strategies are effective if they aim at: minimising opportunities for learning prejudices; changing negative attitudes; de-emphasising narrow social identity based on the ingroup; and discouraging the tendency towards self-fulfilling prophecy among victims of prejudice.
Education and information dissemination: correcting stereotypes about specific target groups and tackling strong ingroup bias.

Increasing intergroup contact (the contact hypothesis): direct communication removes mistrust and helps groups discover positive qualities in each other. It works best when the groups meet in a cooperative rather than competitive context, interact closely, and are not different in power or status.
Working towards shared, superordinate goals that neither group can achieve alone encourages cooperation and reduces ingroup–outgroup hostility.
Highlighting individual identity rather than group identity weakens the importance of group membership as a basis for judging others.

example.q: A college finds tension between students from two hostels. Suggest two strategies based on psychology.
steps: Create mixed teams for a project both hostels need to complete (cooperative contact with a superordinate goal).
Run information sessions correcting stereotypes each hostel holds about the other.
Encourage students to know each other as individuals, not just as 'Hostel A' or 'Hostel B'.
example.answer: Cooperative intergroup contact with shared goals, education to correct stereotypes, and emphasising individual identity.

learn.reallife: India's school exchange programmes — students from different states living with host families — use the contact hypothesis to build understanding across regions and languages.

quiz.explain: Both are true; when these conditions are missing, contact can even increase hostility.
steps: A: contact does not always reduce prejudice – true.
R: it works mainly in cooperative, close, equal-status contact – true.
Without those conditions contact can fail.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks any contact automatically reduces prejudice.

quiz.q: Which situation best applies the contact hypothesis?
options: Two rival colleges compete for one trophy with no interaction
Students from two rival colleges form mixed teams to organise a joint relief drive
Students from one college hear rumours about the other
Each college is told to avoid the other
quiz.explain: Cooperative, close interaction with a shared goal fits the contact hypothesis.
steps: Mixed teams from rival colleges organising a joint relief drive.
That gives close, cooperative contact with a shared goal.
Answer: Students from two rival colleges form mixed teams to organise a joint relief drive

quiz.q: Case: A company with tension between two departments makes them jointly responsible for a product launch that needs both teams' skills. Which strategy is being used?
options: Superordinate goals with cooperative intergroup contact
quiz.explain: A shared goal that needs both groups encourages cooperation and reduces prejudice.
steps: Two departments jointly responsible for a launch needing both.
That is a superordinate goal with cooperative intergroup contact.
Answer: Superordinate goals with cooperative intergroup contact
quiz.mistake: Picks a source of prejudice instead of a strategy.

teach.praise: Tweet! Bring them together cooperatively, give them a shared goal, and help them see each other as individuals!

revise.summary: Prejudice is handled by limiting opportunities to learn it, changing negative attitudes, de-emphasising narrow ingroup identity and discouraging self-fulfilling prophecy. Methods: education, intergroup contact (under the right conditions), superordinate goals and stressing individual identity.
focus: The four aims of strategies against prejudice
remember: Contact hypothesis works with cooperative context, close interaction, similar status
Superordinate goal: achievable only by both groups together
Highlight individual identity over group identity
traps: Contact alone, in competition, can increase hostility
Superordinate does not mean one group above another
Keeping groups apart does not reduce prejudice
